source_text: Οὕτω καὶ περὶ τῆς γλώττης λογισώμεθα· ξίφος ἐστὶν ἐν μέσῳ κείμενον· ἀκόνησον οὖν αὐτὴν κατὰ τῆς τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων τῶν σῶν κατηγορίας· μὴ κατὰ ἀδελφοῦ τὴν πληγὴν ὠθήσῃς. Διὰ τοῦτο διπλῷ τειχίῳ περιέβαλεν αὐτὴν ὁ Θεὸς, τῷ τῶν ὀδόντων διαφράγματι καὶ τῇ τῶν χειλέων περιβολῇ, ἵνα μὴ ῥᾳδίως καὶ ἀπερισκέπτως ἐκφέρῃ τὰ ῥήματα τὰ μὴ προσήκοντα. Χαλίνωσον αὐτὴν ἔνδον. Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀνέχεται; καὶ σωφρόνισον αὐτὴν διὰ τῶν ὀδόντων, ὥσπερ δημίοις τούτοις ἐκδοὺς αὐτῆς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ ποιήσας δακεῖν· καὶ γὰρ βέλτιον αὐτὴν δηχθῆναι τοῖς ὀδοῦσι νῦν ἁμαρτάνουσαν, ἢ τότε ζητοῦσαν σταγόνα ὕδατος καὶ τηγανιζομένην μὴ τυχεῖν τῆς παραμυθίας. Πολλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἄλλα ἁμαρτάνειν εἴωθε λοιδοροῦσα, βλασφημοῦσα, αἰσχρὰ προϊεμένη ῥήματα, συκοφαντοῦσα, ὀμνύουσα, ἐπιορκοῦσα. εʹ. Ἀλλ' ἵνα μὴ πάντα ἀθρόον τήμερον ὑμῖν λέγοντες καταχώσωμεν ὑμῶν τὴν διάνοιαν, ἕνα τέως τίθεμεν ὑμῖν νόμον τὸν περὶ τῆς τῶν ὅρκων φυλακῆς, ἐκεῖνο προλέγοντες καὶ διαγορεύοντες, ὅτι εἰ μὴ φύγητε τοὺς ὅρκους, οὐ λέγω τὰς ἐπιορκίας μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἐπὶ τῷ δικαίῳ γινομένους εἰ μὴ φύγητε, οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἑτέρας ὑποθέσεως ὑμῖν διαλεξόμεθα. Καὶ γὰρ ἄτοπον τοὺς μὲν τῶν γραμμάτων διδασκάλους μὴ δεύτερον τοῖς παιδίοις διδόναι μάθημα, ἕως ἂν τὸ πρότερον ἴδωσι καλῶς ἐμπαγὲν αὐτῶν τῇ μνήμῃ· ἡμᾶς δὲ τὰ πρότερον μαθήματα μὴ δυναμένους ἀπαγγεῖλαι μετὰ ἀκριβείας, ἕτερα προεμβαλεῖν πάλιν· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἕτερον τοῦτο, ἀλλ' ἢ εἰς πίθον τετρημένον ἀντλεῖν. Ἵνα οὖν ἡμᾶς μὴ ἐπιστομίσητε, πολλὴν τοῦ πράγματος ποιήσασθε τὴν σπουδήν. Καὶ γὰρ χαλεπὸν τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ ἁμάρτημα, καὶ σφόδρα χαλεπόν· σφόδρα δέ ἐστι χαλεπὸν, ὅτι οὐ δοκεῖ χαλεπὸν εἶναι, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸ δέδοικα, ἐπειδὴ οὐδεὶς αὐτὸ δέδοικε· διὰ τοῦτο ἀνίατόν ἐστι τὸ νόσημα, ἐπειδὴ οὐδὲ νόσημα εἶναι δοκεῖ· ἀλλ' ὥσπερ τὸ διαλέγεσθαι ἁπλῶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἔγκλημα, οὕτως οὐδὲ τοῦτο ἔγκλημα εἶναι δοκεῖ, ἀλλὰ μετὰ πολλῆς παῤῥησίας ἡ παρανομία αὕτη τολμᾶται· κἂν ἐγκαλέσῃ τις, εὐθέως γέλως ἕπεται καὶ χλευασία πολλὴ, οὐχὶ τοῖς ἐγκαλουμένοις ὑπὲρ τῶν ὅρκων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς διορθῶσαι τὸ νόσημα βουλομένοις. Διὰ τοῦτο μακρὸν ὑπὲρ τούτων ἀποτείνω τὸν λόγον· βαθεῖαν γὰρ ῥίζαν ἀνασπάσαι βούλομαι, καὶ χρόνιον ἀπαλεῖψαι κακόν· οὐ λέγω τὰς ἐπιορκίας μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς εὐορκίας αὐτάς. Ἀλλ' ὁ δεῖνα, φησὶν, ἄνθρωπος ἐπιεικὴς, εἰς ἱερωσύνην τελῶν, πολλῇ σωφροσύνῃ καὶ εὐλαβείᾳ συζῶν. Μή μοι τὸν ἐπιεικῆ τοῦτον εἴπῃς, τὸν σώφρονα, τὸν εὐλαβῆ, τὸν εἰς ἱερωσύνην τελοῦντα· ἀλλ', εἰ βούλει, θὲς Πέτρον εἶναι τοῦτον ἢ Παῦλον, ἢ καὶ ἄγγελον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καταβάντα· οὐδὲ γὰρ οὕτως ἐπιστρέφομαι πρὸς τὴν ἀξίαν τῶν προσώπων. Νόμον γὰρ οὐχὶ δουλικὸν, ἀλλὰ βασιλικὸν ἀναγινώσκω ἐγὼ τὸν περὶ τῶν ὅρκων· ὅταν δὲ βασιλέως ἀναγινώσκηται γράμματα, ἅπαν τὸ τῶν δούλων ἀξίωμα ἡσυχαζέτω. Ἂν μὲν γὰρ ἔχῃς εἰπεῖν, ὅτι ὁ Χριστὸς ὀμνύναι ἐκέλευσεν, ἢ ὅτι ὁ Χριστὸς οὐ κολάζει τοῦτο γινόμενον, δεῖξον καὶ πείθομαι· εἰ δὲ μετὰ τοσαύτης ἀπείργει σπουδῆς, καὶ τοσαύτην ὑπὲρ τοῦ πράγματος ποιεῖται πρόνοιαν, ὡς μετὰ τοῦ Πονηροῦ στῆσαι τὸν ὀμνύοντα Τὸ γὰρ περισσὸν τούτων, τοῦ ναὶ, καὶ τοῦ οὒ, φησὶν, ἐκ τοῦ διαβόλου ἐστὶ, τί μοι τὸν δεῖνα καὶ τὸν δεῖνα προσάγεις εἰς μέσον; Οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς ῥᾳθυμίας τῶν συνδούλων οἴσει σοι τὴν ψῆφον ὁ Θεὸς ταύτην, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς ἐπιταγῆς τῶν αὑτοῦ νόμων.
thought_title: The tongue as a sword and the law against oaths
orientation: John Chrysostom is addressing the catechumens, continuing his instruction on mastering the tongue and now laying down a single law for them: to renounce all oaths.
pass_a_gloss: So let us reason also about the tongue. It is a sword lying in the middle. Sharpen it, then, against the accusation of your own sins. Do not thrust the blow against a brother. For this reason God surrounded it with a double wall, with the barrier of the teeth and the enclosure of the lips, so that it may not easily and thoughtlessly utter words that are not fitting. Bridle it within. But it does not submit? Discipline it also by means of the teeth, as if handing over its body to these executioners, and making it bite. For it is better for it to be bitten by the teeth now when it sins, than then when it seeks a drop of water and is being roasted not to obtain the consolation. Many other sins, then, it is accustomed to commit: reviling, blaspheming, uttering shameful words, slandering, swearing oaths, committing perjury. 5. But so that we may not, by saying everything to you all at once today, bury your mind, we lay down for you for the present one law, the one about the guarding against oaths, declaring and proclaiming beforehand that if you do not flee oaths—I do not mean perjuries only, but also the oaths that are made for a just cause—if you do not flee them, we will no longer discuss another subject with you. For it is absurd that teachers of letters do not give a second lesson to the children until they see the first one well fixed in their memory, but that we, when you are not able to recite the earlier lessons with accuracy, should throw in other things again. For this is nothing other than drawing water into a pierced jar. So that you may not stop our mouths, then, make great diligence about this matter. For this sin is hard, and very hard. And it is very hard because it does not seem to be hard, and for this reason I fear it, because no one fears it. For this reason the disease is incurable, because it does not even seem to be a disease. But just as conversing simply is not a charge, so neither does this seem to be a charge, but with great boldness this lawlessness is dared. And if someone brings a charge, immediately laughter follows and much mockery, not against those who are accused concerning the oaths, but against those who wish to correct the disease. For this reason I stretch out my discourse at length about these things. For I wish to pull up a deep root, and to wipe away a long-standing evil. I do not mean perjuries only, but also truthful oaths themselves. But so-and-so, someone says, is a decent man, one who is enrolled for the priesthood, living with much self-control and piety. Do not tell me about this decent man, the self-controlled one, the pious one, the one enrolled for the priesthood. But, if you wish, suppose that this man is Peter or Paul, or even an angel come down from heaven. For not even so do I turn toward the dignity of persons. For I read a law that is not servile but royal, the law about oaths. And when the letters of a king are read, let all the dignity of servants be silent. For if you can say that Christ commanded swearing oaths, or that Christ does not punish this when it happens, show it and I am persuaded. But if he forbids it with so much diligence, and makes so much provision about the matter, as to place the one who swears with the Evil One—for 'what is more than these, than the yes and the no,' he says, 'is from the devil'—why do you bring so-and-so and so-and-so into the middle? For God will not bring this vote to you from the negligence of your fellow servants, but from the command of his own laws.

choices.term: ἀκόνησον οὖν αὐτὴν κατὰ τῆς τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων τῶν σῶν κατηγορίας
choices.english: Sharpen it, then, against the accusation of your own sins
choices.why: The genitive 'τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων τῶν σῶν' is the object of 'κατηγορίας' (accusation of your sins), and 'κατὰ' with genitive means 'against'; the command is to use the tongue as a weapon against one's own sins, not against a brother.
rejected: Sharpen it against the accusation of your sins
Sharpen it for the accusation of your own sins

choices.why: The dative is instrumental; 'double wall' preserves the metaphor of fortification that Chrysostom develops with the teeth and lips.

choices.term: ὥσπερ δημίοις τούτοις ἐκδοὺς αὐτῆς τὸ σῶμα
choices.english: as if handing over its body to these executioners
choices.why: The dative 'δημίοις' is the recipient of the handing over; 'as if' renders ὥσπερ; 'these' refers to the teeth just mentioned.
rejected: as if giving its body to these executioners
as if delivering its body to these executioners

choices.english: we lay down for you for the present one law
choices.why: The present tense τίθεμεν is a performative declaration; 'for the present' renders τέως, which marks the temporary scope of the single law.
rejected: we set one law for you for now
we establish one law for you for the present

choices.english: drawing water into a pierced jar
choices.why: The infinitive ἀντλεῖν means 'to draw water'; the image is of futile labor, and 'pierced jar' renders τετρημένον πίθον literally.
The verb means 'to silence by stopping the mouth'; the first-person plural object is implied by the context of the preacher's discourse.

pass_b_english: Let us think the same way about the tongue. It is a sword lying in the middle. Sharpen it, then, against the accusation of your own sins, but do not thrust the blow against a brother. For this reason God surrounded it with a double wall—the barrier of the teeth and the enclosure of the lips—so that it may not easily and thoughtlessly utter words that are not fitting. Bridle it within. But it will not submit? Then discipline it with your teeth, as if handing over its body to these executioners and making it bite itself. For it is better for the tongue to be bitten by the teeth now while it is sinning, than to seek a drop of water then, while being roasted, and not obtain that comfort.

The tongue is accustomed to commit many other sins as well: insulting, blaspheming, uttering shameful words, slandering, swearing oaths, committing perjury. But so that we do not bury your mind today by telling you everything at once, we lay down for you for the present one law, the law about guarding against oaths. And we declare and announce this in advance: if you do not flee from oaths—I do not mean only perjury, but even oaths made for a just cause—if you do not flee from them, we will no longer discuss any other subject with you. For it would be absurd if teachers of letters do not give children a second lesson until they see the first one firmly fixed in their memory, but we, unable to deliver the earlier lessons with accuracy, pile on others again. That is nothing other than drawing water from a pierced jar.

So that you may not stop our mouths, make every effort in this matter. For this sin is difficult, exceedingly difficult. And it is exceedingly difficult because it does not seem difficult. This is why I fear it—because no one fears it. This is why the disease is incurable—because it does not even seem to be a disease. Just as ordinary conversation is not a crime, so this does not seem to be a crime either, but this lawlessness is committed with great boldness. And if someone rebukes it, immediately there follows laughter and much mockery—not against those who bring charges concerning oaths, but against those who want to correct the disease. For this reason I stretch out my discourse at length about these things. I want to pull up a deep root and wipe away a long-standing evil. I do not mean only perjury, but even truthful oaths themselves.

But someone says, “That man is decent, he is enrolled for the priesthood, he lives with great self-control and piety.” Do not tell me about this decent man, this self-controlled man, this pious man, this man enrolled for the priesthood. If you wish, suppose that he is Peter or Paul, or even an angel come down from heaven. Even so I do not turn toward the dignity of persons. For the law I read about oaths is not a slave’s law but a king’s law. And when a king’s letters are read, let all the dignity of slaves be silent. If you can say that Christ commanded us to swear, or that Christ does not punish this when it happens, show me and I am persuaded. But if he forbids it with such earnestness and shows such care for the matter that he places the one who swears alongside the Evil One—for “anything more than these, than yes and no,” he says, “is from the devil” (Matthew 5:37)—why do you bring this man or that man into the discussion? God will not render his verdict to you based on the negligence of your fellow servants, but based on the command of his own laws.

problems.quote: drawing water into a pierced jar
problems.why: 'ἀντλεῖν' means 'to draw water from', not 'into'; the image is drawing from a leaky jar—futile effort, not filling.
problems.fix: drawing water from a pierced jar

edits.old: drawing water into a pierced jar
edits.new: drawing water from a pierced jar

fixed: Changed 'into' to 'from' because ἀντλεῖν means to draw water from a source, and the image is of futile labor drawing from a leaky jar.

problems.quote: as if handing over its body to these executioners and making it bite
problems.source_quote: ὥσπερ δημίοις τούτοις ἐκδοὺς αὐτῆς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ ποιήσας δακεῖν
problems.why: ποιήσας δακεῖν means 'making it [the tongue] bite' (reflexive/causative), not 'making it [the teeth] bite'.
problems.fix: as if handing over its body to these executioners and making it bite itself

problems.quote: when you cannot repeat the earlier lessons with accuracy, should pile on still more
problems.source_quote: ἡμᾶς δὲ τὰ πρότερον μαθήματα μὴ δυναμένους ἀπαγγεῖλαι μετὰ ἀκριβείας, ἕτερα προεμβαλεῖν πάλιν
problems.why: μὴ δυναμένους ἀπαγγεῖλαι modifies 'us' (the teachers), not 'you'; 'we, unable to deliver the earlier lessons accurately, pile on others again'.
problems.fix: but we, unable to deliver the earlier lessons with accuracy, pile on others again

problems.quote: not against those who are rebuked for their oaths
problems.source_quote: οὐχὶ τοῖς ἐγκαλουμένοις ὑπὲρ τῶν ὅρκων
problems.why: Source says 'not against those who bring charges concerning oaths'; ἐγκαλουμένοις means 'those who accuse/rebuke', not 'those rebuked'.
problems.fix: not against those who bring charges on behalf of oaths
problems.ruling: ἐγκαλουμένοις is passive 'those accused/rebuked', but context demands 'those who accuse' (rebukers), not 'those rebuked'.

problems.quote: the law about guarding against oaths
problems.source_quote: τὸν περὶ τῆς τῶν ὅρκων φυλακῆς
problems.why: φυλακῆς means 'keeping'/'observance', not 'guarding against'; Chrysostom means keeping the law about oaths.
problems.fix: the law about the keeping of oaths
problems.ruling: φυλακῆς means 'keeping/observance' of oaths, not 'guarding against'; Chrysostom urges keeping the law about oaths.

problems.source_quote: τὸν περὶ τῆς τῶν ὅρκων φυλακῆς
problems.why: φυλακῆς means 'guarding against', not 'keeping'; Chrysostom forbids oaths entirely.
problems.fix: the law about guarding against oaths
problems.ruling: φυλακῆς with φεύγειν means avoiding/fleeing oaths, not keeping them; Chrysostom forbids oaths entirely.

fixed: The English 'the keeping of oaths' misstates the source 'τὸν περὶ τῆς τῶν ὅρκων φυλακῆς', where φυλακῆς means 'guarding against', not 'keeping'; Chrysostom forbids oaths entirely, so the phrase must be 'the law about guarding against oaths'.

refereed.quote: anything more than these, than yes and no
refereed.source_quote: τὸ γὰρ περισσὸν τούτων, τοῦ ναὶ, καὶ τοῦ οὒ
refereed.why: τούτων ('of these') refers to yes and no; 'than these, than' is garbled, suggesting two different comparisons.
refereed.fix: For anything beyond these, of yes and of no
refereed.ruling: περισσὸν τούτων means 'more than these [words]'; 'anything more than these, than yes and no' garbles by making 'yes and no' a second comparison rather than apposition explaining 'these'.
